The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

Sanayi ve Teknoloji Bakanı Mehmet Fatih Kacır, Yapay Zeka Destekli Temiz Teknolojiler Girişimi'nin yenilikçi yapay zeka destekli temiz teknolojilerini pratik uygulamaya geçirmek ve bunların sektörlerle ekonomiler genelinde benimsenmesini hızlandırmak için uluslararası bir platform sağlayacağını belirtti.
Antalya'daki Birleşmiş Milletler (BM) İklim Değişikliği Çerçeve Sözleşmesi 31. Taraflar Konferansı (COP31) kapsamında Yapay Zeka Destekli Temiz Teknolojiler Girişimi Lansmanı düzenlendi.
Kacır, burada yaptığı konuşmada, küresel sera gazı emisyonlarının düşürülmesi için teknolojik yenilik ve bilimsel atılımın yanı sıra verimli ve uygun maliyetli temiz teknolojilerinin yaygınlaştırılması gerektiğini vurguladı.
Yapay zekadaki gelişmelerin yeni nesil bataryalar için gelişmiş malzemelerin keşfini hızlandırdığını belirten Kacır, güneş hücresi teknolojilerinin ve düşük karbonlu sanayi süreçlerinin geliştirilmesine de katkı sağladığını, ayrıca yapay zeka destekli araştırmaların deney ve geliştirme süreçlerini hızlandırarak zaman ve kaynak tasarrufu sağladığını ifade etti.
Kacır, yapay zekanın yenilenebilir enerji alanında da kullanıldığını, dönüşümün enerji sistemlerinde de aynı derecede önemli olduğunu aktardı.
Yapay zeka destekli şebeke yönetimi ve ilgili dijital teknolojilerin sanayi üretiminde yeni güç hatları inşa etmeden 175 gigavata kadar ek iletim kapasitesinin kilidini açabileceğine işaret eden Kacır, mevcut yapay zeka uygulamalarının yaygınlaşmasının 2035'e kadar yıllık karbondioksit emisyonlarını yaklaşık 1,4 milyar ton azaltabileceğini dile getirdi.
Kacır, Türkiye'yi gelişmiş yapay zeka çözümlerinin geliştirildiği, sanayi üretimine entegre edildiği ve uluslararası pazarlara sunulduğu küresel bir merkez haline getirmeyi amaçladıklarının altını çizerek, 2030 Yapay Zeka Eylem Planı'yla iki yılda 10 bin ileri düzey yapay zeka uzmanı ve 100 bin yapay zeka uygulama profesyoneli eğitmeyi hedeflediklerini söyledi.
Yapay zeka ve temiz teknolojilerini Türkiye'nin sanayi kapasitesini güçlendirecek ve ekonomik kalkınmayı destekleyecek stratejik alanlar olarak gördüklerini ifade eden Kacır, "Önceliğimiz yenilikçi çözümlerin ortaya çıkması, sanayi uygulamalarına ulaşması ve daha sürdürülebilir, rekabetçi bir ekonomiye katkıda bulunması için gerekli koşulları oluşturmak. Bu doğrultuda, stratejik teknolojilerde özel sektör yatırımlarını teşvik etmek için önemli kamu kaynaklarını harekete geçiriyoruz." diye konuştu.
Kacır, temiz teknolojilerin ticarileşmesi ve yaygınlaşması için kamu, sanayi, araştırma kurumları ve yatırımcılar arasında güçlü işbirliği gerektiğine dikkati çekerek, şöyle devam etti:
"İşte bu anlayışla, COP31'de Yapay Zeka Destekli Temiz Teknoloji Girişimi'ni başlatıyoruz. Bu girişim, yenilikçi yapay zeka destekli temiz teknolojileri pratik uygulamaya geçirmek ve bunların sektörlerle ekonomiler genelinde benimsenmesini hızlandırmak için uluslararası bir platform sağlayacak. Teknoloji geliştiricilerini sanayi ortakları ve yatırımcılarla buluşturarak pilot projeleri kolaylaştırmayı, ölçülebilir çevresel faydaları göstermeyi ve başarılı çözümlerin daha geniş ölçekte uygulanması için fırsatlar yaratmayı hedefliyoruz."
Hükümetleri, uluslararası kuruluşları, araştırma kurumlarını, sanayi şirketlerini, teknoloji girişimcilerini ve yatırımcıları bu ortak çabaya katkıda bulunmaya davet eden Kacır, iklim sorunlarına çözüm üretecek teknolojiler, pilot uygulamalar, finansman ve teknik uzmanlık alanlarında işbirliğine açık olduklarını dile getirdi.
Kacır, yapay zekanın iklimle mücadele, sürdürülebilir kalkınma ve toplumsal refah için etkili bir araca dönüştürülmesi amacıyla uluslararası işbirliği çağrısında bulundu.
Anadolu Ajansı web sitesinde, AA Haber Akış Sistemi (HAS) üzerinden abonelere sunulan haberler, özetlenerek yayımlanmaktadır. Abonelik için lütfen iletişime geçiniz.
Bu haberde bir hata mı var? Her türlü talep, şikâyet ve görüş için okur temsilcimize ulaşabilirsiniz.

The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.
China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.
Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.
The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.
But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.
As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.
Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."
US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.
Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week , enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.
Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trump during his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.
In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.
Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series , it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.
Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.
But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships , including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.
Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.
China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.
Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.
Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.
"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.
It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."
Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.
A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"
Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.
Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.
The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.
For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."
Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.
"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.
This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.
According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.
China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.
"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.
However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.
Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.
Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.
The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."
According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."
Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."

Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania , it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe .
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government , which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union , with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

Ukraine’s military has been relying on the internet service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia.
Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity.
Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.
Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas.
In a statement on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other.
He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”.
“We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added.
Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days.
This is not the first time Ukrainian officials have complained about limits on Starshield hampering Kyiv’s defence efforts.
Last month, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian missile and drone strikes, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.
According to a November 2 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Starshield is critical to Ukraine since it helps in encrypting satellite communications, which are needed to guide drones in order to carry out interceptions.
“In addition to using Starshield service for strikes within Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, Ukraine uses Starshield-equipped drones to intercept and defend against Russian drones, such as new jet-powered drones taking aim at Ukrainian critical infrastructure and civilian targets,” the CSIS report noted.
Without access to Starshield internet, these Ukrainian drones are unable to work as effectively.
“Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered ‘shaheds’,” Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday.
After last month’s disruptions, Zelenskyy said on X that “intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.
“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he added.
Last month, Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, had posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (161km/h).
That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he had said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.
Officials have said the restrictions have also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.
Jet-powered drones are high-speed uncrewed aerial vehicles equipped with small turbojet engines rather than traditional propellers or piston engines.
In its war on Ukraine, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered variants such as the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 models.
These drones fly at much higher speeds than traditional propeller-powered drones, making them significantly harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept.
In August, 38 people were killed in the village of Myla in Ukraine, when a Russian drone attack struck an ammunition depot. Another 12 were killed in attacks across the country in September.
Ukraine’s Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said in September that while the country has an interception rate of more than 90 percent against propeller-powered drones, that success rate falls to only 60 percent against jet-powered models.
Ukraine has, however, retaliated using its own drone systems, and has also struck Russian refineries, hitting 12 in August, along with two gas-processing plants and three oil shipment terminals, according to its defence ministry.
On Sunday, Ukraine’s army said it also shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.
But to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones more efficiently, Zelenskyy said he had told teams of Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and the presidential office “to work as closely as possible with the American side and SpaceX” and remove restrictions on Starshield.
“It is important to be on the right side of history. It is essential to help Ukraine,” he said on Sunday.
Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, is yet to respond to recent accusations about Starshield from Zelenskyy.
But last month, the company and Musk denied restricting internet speeds.
Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote last month, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.
Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times last month that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.
The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.
Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Donald Trump returned to the presidency last year, including over Washington’s increasing reluctance to militarily support Ukraine and its mounting efforts to forge a deal with Russia.
But Trump has said that it is Musk who controls Starlink’s operations in Ukraine.
When asked about internet restrictions in Ukraine, he told reporters last month that Musk had restored Kyiv’s access, while denying any White House role in the episode.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said last month that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.
“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠⁠⁠⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio had said.
Meanwhile, officials from Ukraine and Russia held peace talks in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, last week. The talks, mediated by the US, only yielded an agreement on a prisoner exchange and failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark.
The US, however, pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join NATO, an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means…

Şirketten yapılan açıklamaya göre, Türk Telekom, COP31'de üstlendiği küresel dijital dönüşüm ve teknoloji destekçiliği kapsamında zirvenin dijital altyapısını uçtan uca yönetiyor.
Bu kapsamda, Türk Telekom, güçlü fiber ve mobil altyapısı, yeni nesil teknolojileri ve mühendislik birikimiyle uluslararası katılımcıları Antalya'dan dünyaya bağlıyor.
Türk Telekom, 1,1 milyon metrekarelik zirve alanında 1,3 milyon metre fiber hat, 400 Gbps bağlantı kapasitesi, 1800 kablosuz erişim noktası ve 18 mobil baz istasyonuyla organizasyonun dijital ihtiyaçlarını karşılıyor.
Türk Telekom'un teknoloji gücü ve operasyonel kabiliyetini zirvenin ilk haftasında gerçekleşen dijital iletişim verileri de ortaya koydu.
COP31'in ilk haftasında toplam 380 terabaytlık (TB) veri trafiği gerçekleşirken, mobil şebeke üzerinden 130 TB'lık kullanım, sabit ağ üzerinden ise 250 TB veri trafiği kaydedildi.
Zirvede, Birleşmiş Milletler'in liderler zirvesi etkinliklerine ev sahipliği yapan Mavi Bölge'de eş zamanlı bağlı cihaz sayısı da 27 bin 794'e ulaşarak, COP organizasyonları tarihindeki en yüksek seviyeye çıktı.
Açıklamada görüşlerine yer verilen Türk Telekom CEO'su Ebubekir Şahin, Türk Telekom'un 185 yılı aşkın geçmişinden aldıkları güç ve birikimle Türkiye'nin dijital geleceğini inşa etme sorumluluğunu kararlılıkla sürdürdüklerini belirtti.
Şahin, Türkiye'nin teknoloji alanındaki potansiyelini küresel platformlara taşımayı, yerli mühendislik gücüyle teknolojik yetkinlikleri uluslararası ölçekte görünür kılmayı önemsediklerini vurguladı.
"Yarına Sözümüz Var" yaklaşımıyla dijital dönüşümün sunduğu fırsatları toplumun tüm kesimleri için değere dönüştürdüklerini anlatan Şahin, teknolojinin daha sürdürülebilir bir geleceğe katkı sağlamasına öncülük ettiklerini aktardı.
Şahin, bu vizyon doğrultusunda COP31 gibi tüm dünyanın takip ettiği bir organizasyonun Küresel Dijital Dönüşüm ve Teknoloji destekçisi olmaktan gurur duyduklarının altını çizerek, şunları kaydetti:
"Geleceğimizin şekilleneceği bu küresel organizasyonda yalnızca iletişim altyapısını sağlayan bir operatör olarak değil, mühendislik gücümüz, enerji verimliliğine odaklanan yenilikçi çözümlerimiz, operasyonel yetkinliğimiz ve sürdürülebilirlik vizyonumuzla sürecin önemli paydaşlarından biri olarak yer alıyoruz. Fiber ve mobil ağımızdan yeni nesil bağlantı teknolojilerine, veri merkezi kapasitemizden, network ve siber güvenlik operasyonlarına uzanan bütüncül bir sistemle zirvenin dijital ihtiyaçları için yüksek kapasite, hız ve güvenlik sunuyoruz. Dünya Antalya'da iklim değişikliğini ve geleceği konuşurken, zirvedeki bu konuşmaları teknoloji gücümüzle Antalya'dan tüm dünyaya taşıyoruz. Bu büyük operasyonu kesintisiz ve güvenilir biçimde sürdürmek için 2 bin arkadaşımız sahada görev yapıyor."
Organizasyonun ilk haftasında ortaya çıkan kullanım verilerinin de şirketin teknoloji yatırımlarının, güçlü altyapının ve operasyonel yetkinliğinin somut bir göstergesi niteliğinde olduğuna işaret eden Şahin, Türkiye'nin teknoloji alanındaki birikimini ve dijital yetkinliğini her alanda güçlü biçimde temsil etmeyi sürdüreceklerini ifade etti.

Russell Brand (pictured during his trial) delivered a message to followers via his wife Laura
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.
The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".
In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.
"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."
In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.
Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".
She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".
Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.
Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."
Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."
"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.
Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.
"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."
While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".
She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.
If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.
Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.
This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.

Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.
Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.
She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.
Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.
In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...
"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."
But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.
Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.
She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".
Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'".
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.
Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".
Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.
"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."
Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.
The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.
The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.

Apple , insanların sağlıkla ilgili sorularını yapay zeka araçlarıyla nasıl yanıtladığını incelemek amacıyla yeni bir araştırma başlattı . Şirket, sağlık alanında yapay zeka çözümleri geliştiren OpenEvidence ile iş birliği yaparak bu araştırma için özel bir uygulama hazırladı. 12 aydan uzun sürmesi planlanan araştırmaya 200 bine kadar katılımcının dahil edilmesi hedefleniyor.
Apple'ın araştırması, yapay zekanın sağlık alanındaki kullanımını ve kullanıcıların bu araçlardan nasıl yararlandığını anlamaya odaklanıyor. Bu kapsamda geliştirilen uygulama, ChatGPT ve Claude gibi sohbet botlarına benzer şekilde kullanıcıların sağlıkla ilgili sorularını yanıtlıyor. Ancak uygulamanın yanıtları The New England Journal of Medicine , Journal of the American Medical Association ve Nature gibi yayınlarda yer alan klinik verilere dayanıyor.
Kullanıcılar, aldıkları yanıtları puanlayabiliyor ve geri bildirimde bulunabiliyor. Ayrıca araştırmaya katılanlardan her ay anketleri yanıtlamaları isteniyor. Katılımcılar, daha kişiselleştirilmiş yanıtlar alabilmek için dinlenme kalp atış hızı, fiziksel aktivite, uyku ve laboratuvar sonuçları gibi Apple HealthKit verilerini de uygulamayla paylaşabiliyor. Uygulama, kullanıcıların doktor randevularına hazırlanmasına yardımcı olmanın yanı sıra endişe verici sağlık sorunlarında ilgili uzmanlara yönlendirme yapabiliyor.
Araştırmaya ABD'de yaşayan 21 yaşından büyük, iPhone 15 veya daha yeni bir model kullanan, iOS 26 ve üzeri işletim sistemine sahip ve Apple Intelligence özelliğini etkinleştirmiş kişiler katılabiliyor. Uygulama, ABD'deki kullanıcılar tarafından bugünden itibaren indirilebiliyor.
Apple, araştırma kapsamında toplanan verilerin güvenli bir üçüncü taraf bulut sağlayıcısına gönderilmeden önce anonim hale getirileceğini ve herhangi bir yapay zeka modelini eğitmek için kullanılmayacağını belirtiyor. OpenEvidence ise kullanıcıların sorularını ve bu sorulara verilen yanıtları 24 saat sonra silecek.
Apple, araştırmadan elde edilecek bulguların sağlık alanında güvenilir yapay zeka araçlarının geliştirilmesine katkı sağlamasını bekliyor. Şirketin bu sonuçları Sağlık uygulaması veya Siri'ye yeni özellikler eklemek için kullanıp kullanmayacağı ise henüz bilinmiyor. OpenAI, yılın başında ChatGPT'ye her hafta sağlıkla ilgili 300 milyondan fazla soru yöneltildiğini açıklamıştı .

Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”
Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.
“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.
US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.
Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

Gérard Depardieu appeared at a courthouse in Paris on Monday for his appeal trial that was due to start
French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault , admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.
On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.
"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.
It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.
"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court.
"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.
In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.
"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.
"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.
"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."
The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.
Depardieu's lawyers David-Olivier Kaminski (L) and Delphine Meillet (R) were at the courthouse on Monday for the opening day of their client's appeal trial in Paris
His new lawyers, Delphine Meillet and David-Olivier Kaminski, said that with his admission of guilt Depardieu wanted to "move on", adding that "basically, as he turns 78 years old, he is saying to himself that life is more beautiful than 10 days of court hearings".
In the original trial, Depardieu was said to have touched the two women on intimate parts of the body during the making of Les Volets Verts, which is a film about an ageing actor coming to terms with his declining powers.
He himself admitted to using vulgar language but denied being "a metro-train groper". However, he also said he did not consider touching a woman's buttocks to be an act of "sexual aggression".
The trial was the first time the star of films like Green Card and Cyrano de Bergerac appeared in court on sexual assault charges. Several other women have made similar allegations in the media.
A decision on whether an alleged rape case can come to trial is expected this month.
Gérard Depardieu to face trial over rape and sexual assault allegations

French actor apologises to two women he was convicted of assaulting on a film set in 2021
The French actor Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set, and has for the first time apologised to the victims.
“I was found guilty. I hear it and I accept this conviction,” Depardieu, 77, said in a written statement. “I address my deep and sincere apologies to those who suffered.”
The actor, who has made more than 200 films and TV series, wrote: “For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour.”
He said he accepted that remarks and “some of my gestures” were not “without consequences”, particularly because he held a powerful position in the entertainment industry.
Depardieu said he had never intended to hurt the women he encountered but had “come to understand that intention changes nothing about the harm caused”.
He said times had changed and that he belonged “to a world that no longer exists”.
At a trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021.
His suspended sentence will now stand and his name must be added to France’s sex offender register.
The set dresser, named in the media as Amélie, said outside the Paris appeal court on Monday: “I waited for years for this apology.” She said she would have preferred if Depardieu had attended court to deliver it in person.
The assistant director, named in the media as Sarah, said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”
Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France . He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.
Depardieu had previously denied all allegations of sexual assault. He told last year’s trial that the media had used allegations against him to damage his reputation.
He attacked the #MeToo movement as well as women who had staged protests outside venues during his concert tour at the time of the allegations. “This movement is going to become a terror,” he said.
The trial also set an important legal precedent when the judge ruled that Depardieu’s defence lawyer, Jérémie Assous, had been “excessively harsh” to the two women in court, saying they were not real victims and were liars.
Assous had said the women were working for the cause of “rabid feminism” and called their lawyers hysterical, “abject and stupid” and described them as having an “unbearable voice”.
The judge awarded the complainants compensation for being further victimised by Depardieu’s defence during the trial, ordering Depardieu to pay each woman €1,000 (£835).
The court had heard there was a “system of impunity” around Depardieu, with film industry insiders staying silent to keep cashing in on his name.
Depardieu has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.
In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.
In December 2023, when Depardieu was under formal investigation for rape and sexual assault in the Arnould case and also facing scrutiny over sexist comments revealed in a TV documentary, the French president defended him, saying “he makes France proud”.
Asked at the time about stripping Depardieu of a state award, Emmanuel Macron said: “You will never see me participate in a manhunt … I hate that type of thing.”

Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.
Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured territory overlooking it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may meet with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un in China this week.
Trump made the comments while speaking to reporters as he departed the White House to begin his trip to Asia, which will see him arrive in the Philippines early on Tuesday.
The president is then set to travel on to China, where he is scheduled to take part in trilateral talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also," Trump told the media. "So that would be good. We have the chance to accomplish a lot."
Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen in southeastern China this week, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
"We're going to talk about denuclearisation. Tough subject because it's very hard for any of us say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said on Monday. "Especially since you do have other countries."
He added that the wars in Iran and Ukraine would also come up, as well as "economics and trade."
In August, Trump talked up his relationship with Kim and said the pair would meet at some point in the year, although he gave no further details.
"The fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," the president said at the time, adding: "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."

PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’
The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction .
Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”
If found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a telephone for a limited period.
It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.
Asked about the comments, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.
“Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken.”
Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.
In his message, Brand said he had been moved from the category-B Wandsworth prison in south-west London to the category-C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison for men convicted of sexual offences.
Reading the message from a notebook, Laura Brand said: “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.
“I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.
“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for and forgive one another as God forgave us.”
Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, meaning that no criminal offence has been committed in the release of the podcast. They are not, however, allowed to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media.
According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”
The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.
Mia Latter, who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and has waived her right to anonymity, said his message was an “insult” to his victims and questioned why YouTube had allowed the video to be shared.
She told The Jeremy Vine Show on Channel 5: “I was shocked that YouTube put it out, because I feel like they have some kind of responsibility not to let these things be broadcast.
“And, it was an insult to all the women that stood trial, and it was an insult to the jurors that gave their time. It’s an insult to the criminal justice system.”
In July 2022, prisoner Charles Bronson said he was given a 28-day phone ban after sending an unauthorised voice note from his cell at HMP Woodhill.
Prison sources said it was not yet clear whether Brand had broken a rule because the message was posted by Brand’s wife, not by him, and the material may have been written before conviction. “There are a lot of possible scenarios, and the full facts are still to emerge,” a source said.
Responding to the video on Monday, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.”
According to official guidance, prisoners are expected to make a formal application through their governor if they wish to contact the media.
Allegations against Brand and fellow comedian David Walliams have prompted conversations about introducing a staggered age of consent.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said there was “some common sense” in the idea, but expressed doubts about how it could be enforced.
“I do think that there’s some common sense there in terms of a staggered age of consent. My issue is with how we will enforce it,” she told a press conference. Walliams denies wrongdoing.

Houthi fighters are edging closer to the temporary capital following a sudden withdrawal of government-aligned forces from the Bab al-Mandeb area.
Forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government face a potentially catastrophic situation, as Houthi forces advance on the southern city of Aden and other strategic areas.
Yemeni government forces said on Sunday they had withdrawn from Dhubab airport and territory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, southwest of Yemen, to defend Aden, the de facto seat of the government.
Retired Lebanese Brigadier-General Hassan Jouni, a military and strategic expert, said fighting is now focused on control over a mountainous triangle of territory in southern Yemen, which could decide the outcome of the war.
This area links Aden to Taiz, another city held by the government but encircled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – and Bab al-Mandeb, a maritime chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
“This triangle is the strategic centre of gravity for the war in Yemen as a whole,” Jouni told Al Jazeera.
On Sunday, government-aligned forces were withdrawn from Dhubab, which was recaptured from the Houthis in September, to avoid an imminent siege in the coastal strip by the Houthis and to help defend Aden, analysts say.
Houthi advances in this southwestern region now threaten to completely cut off the government’s coastal supply routes, Jouni said.
The Yemen war began when the Houthis, a Zaidi Shia group close to Iran, captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south to Aden. Saudi Arabia launched an Arab coalition military campaign to aid the government in March 2015, launching thousands of air strikes against Houthi forces.
Following a relatively peaceful few years, fighting re-erupted in July when government forces’ jets bombed Sanaa international airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital.
A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha . Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat from Dhubab, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.
“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.
But Jouni believes the situation faced by government forces is grim, with the Houthis reaching Tor al-Baha, just 80km (50 miles) from Aden.
“The Houthi forces have reached this line, meaning that they are indeed in the defensive line area of the city of Aden. We do not say they have approached Aden, but the defence of the city of Aden begins in this area,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The basic combat direction now is in the vicinity of the besieged city of Taiz. On the other hand, of course, the Houthis will focus their attention now on approaching Aden and controlling the first defensive zone.”
Strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab gave a less optimistic assessment of the situation than the one presented by the government.
“What happened is a retreat or a withdrawal with the same meaning, and not a redeployment, because the withdrawal left a vast vacuum filled by the Houthis,” al-Dahab stated.
The government’s “Operation Yemen Dawn” has responded to the situation with a dramatic increase in strikes on Houthi positions, including 900 targeting operations within 24 hours.
The Houthis have responded with ballistic missiles and drone attacks towards Mecca, Riyadh, and the Eastern province in Saudi Arabia. They have announced they will continue operations under a principle of “siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation”.
Al-Dahab said this strategy is directed at Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s key international ally, and not at authorities in Aden.
With their recent gains on the coast along Bab al-Mandeb, which has become increasingly significant to global maritime trade since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran, the Houthis have significant geopolitical leverage.
“They now directly and completely control the western Yemeni coastal sector and part of the maritime extension towards Aden,” al-Dahab warned.
“The matter translates the Houthis’ gains in Bab al-Mandeb in large part to the benefit of Iran.”

Two Israeli opposition leaders denounced an "attempted coup" on Monday following press reports that outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office tried to frame members of an Arab-Israeli party ahead of last month's election.
"As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn't an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup," Yair Lapid, who headed the opposition in the previous legislature and co-chairs the Beyachad list, wrote on X.
Israel's Channel 12 television reported on Sunday that on the eve of the 27 October election, Netanyahu's chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.
Norden reportedly pointed the police to a purported intelligence source, a former employee of Netanyahu's office, who provided information that led to the arrest of three Raam members.
The three men were later released when the police determined that the information was unfounded.
Netanyahu subsequently accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats. His Likud party issued a statement denying the latest allegations.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz also reported that David Zini, head of the Shin Bet domestic security service, sought to wiretap leaders of the other Arab slate, the Joint List, but the attorney general turned down his request due to lack of evidence.
Following the report, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also denounced an "attempted coup by Netanyahu".
"If the findings are confirmed, this is a criminal mechanism that operated from the heart of government to rig the election results. Everyone found responsible must be held accountable, including Netanyahu," he wrote on X.
Raam's number two, former police chief Yoav Segalovitz, called for an urgent investigation.
"These suspicions require an immediate, independent and thorough criminal investigation that reaches everyone involved, at every level and in every role," he wrote on X.
"Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now," he added.
Netanyahu's main rival, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer".
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month's election.
The two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog with forming a government.

Romelu Lukaku scored three goals for Belgium at the World Cup this summer
Romelu Lukaku has retired from international football, saying he has "enjoyed every single moment" of playing for Belgium.
Fenerbahce striker Lukaku, 33, made his international debut in 2010 and is Belgium's all-time leading men's goalscorer with 94 goals in 135 appearances.
He is the fifth highest men's international goalscorer of all time, behind Sunil Chhetri, Ali Daei, Lionel Messi and leader Cristiano Ronaldo, who has scored 146.
Lukaku scored eight goals across four World Cups, including in the run to the quarter-finals at this summer's tournament, and a total of six goals at three European Championships.
Writing on Instagram, , external the former Everton, Chelsea and Manchester United forward thanked his team-mates and coaches "for pushing and trusting me to help the team" during his 16 years with the national side.
He missed Belgium's Nations League win over Turkey last week with a hip injury and was an unused substitute on Sunday as they qualified for the last eight of the competition by beating Italy 4-1.
"These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team... I went through every emotion possible," Lukaku wrote.
"To the Belgium fans thank you for the support you gave our team. I am proud to have represented my country in four World Cups and three European Championships.
"I will never forget those moments. I'm at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing. It was enjoyable. I'm grateful."
In 2023, Lukaku scored 14 times in eight Euro 2024 qualifying appearances, breaking the record for goals scored by a player in a European Championship qualifying campaign.
His Belgium team-mate Kevin de Bruyne posted an image of himself with Lukaku , external on Instagram adding: "There are no words to describe what you've meant to me and our country!"

Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time leading goalscorer, has announced his retirement from international football after 16 years, saying he was “at peace” with his decision.
“These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team. It was a nice ride and I enjoyed every single moment,” Belgium’s record goalscorer said on Instagram on Monday.
With 94 goals in 135 games, Lukaku is the fifth-highest scorer in men’s international football history and featured in four World Cups for the Red Devils, helping them reach the quarterfinals of this year’s tournament before losing to eventual winners Spain.
The 33-year-old, who now plays for Turkish club Fenerbahce, made his debut in 2010 as a teenager and was an unused substitute in Sunday’s 4-1 Nations League win over Italy.
“To the Belgium fans, thank you for the support you gave our team. I am proud to have represented my country in 4 World Cups and 3 European Championships.
“I will never forget those moments. I’m at peace with my decision to stop here,” Lukaku said.
The former Chelsea, Manchester United and Inter Milan forward was part of Belgium’s so-called “golden generation”.
Lukaku, alongside Kevin De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, finished third at the 2018 World Cup, a best-ever finish for Belgium in the tournament, but they failed to lift a trophy during the period.
“I played with amazing teammates that I will always be grateful for,” Lukaku said.
“I want to thank them all. I want to thank all the coaches as well for pushing and trusting me to help the team,” he added.
The national team paid homage to Lukaku shortly after his announcement.
“More than a goalscorer, you have been a leader, a strong personality and an inspiration to generations of Belgian football fans,” said a post on Instagram by the Red Devils. “You have written an incredible chapter in the history of the Red Devils.”
A host of fellow Belgian players also paid tribute to Lukaku.
“Legend, my brother,” midfielder Axel Witsel posted on Instagram.
“So many amazing memories,” the Real Madrid goalkeeper added.
Lukaku’s last appearance for his country came in October’s 4-1 loss to France.
“Beyond his exceptional performances on the pitch, he has been a true leader, with a strong personality and an essential role in the dressing room,” Lukaku’s former teammate and now Belgium’s technical director, Simon Mignolet, said in a statement from the Belgian football association.
“We respect his decision and are deeply grateful to him for everything he has brought to our national team,” the former Liverpool goalkeeper added.
Belgium’s first game without Lukaku will be a Nations League last-eight fixture in March.
“We must now turn our attention to the future and prepare for the Nations League quarterfinals … with the ambition of continuing to make progress as a team,” Mignolet said.
